answer_ref: Dear Client,Domestic violence in India is covered under several laws, primarily under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), and the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Section 498A and Section 352 of the IPC address specific aspects of domestic violence.Understanding the Sections:Section 498A IPC:Objective: To protect married women from cruelty by their husbands and in-laws.Definition: It covers any willful conduct that is likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury to her life, limb, or health (whether mental or physical). It also includes harassment with the aim of coercing her or her relatives to meet any unlawful demand for property or valuable security.Punishment: Imprisonment for up to three years and a fine.Section 352 IPC:Objective: To address assault or use of criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation.Definition: It penalizes the act of assault or use of criminal force against any person without grave and sudden provocation by that person.Punishment: Imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine of up to five hundred rupees, or both.Determining the Applicability:Section 498A: If the case involves a married woman being subjected to cruelty by her husband or in-laws, particularly with respect to harassment for dowry or inflicting harm that could cause serious mental or physical trauma, then it falls under Section 498A.Section 352: If the situation involves an incident where assault or use of criminal force occurred without grave provocation but does not fit the specific criteria of cruelty in a matrimonial context as described in Section 498A, it might fall under Section 352.
answer_pred:
Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) pertains to cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards a woman, often encompassing domestic violence, while Section 352 deals with assault or use of criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation. If the case involves cruelty or harassment by a husband or his relatives, it likely falls under Section 498A. However, if it involves a more general assault without the specific context of marital cruelty, Section 352 may apply.

Legally, the user should determine the nature of the allegations to identify the correct section. If the case is under Section 498A, it is a cognizable and non-bailable offense, requiring immediate legal assistance. If under Section 352, it is a bailable offense, allowing for easier bail procedures. The user should consult with a lawyer to clarify the charges and consider applying for anticipatory bail if under Section 498A.

After the amendment of the Prevention of Corruption Act, in 2018, it significantly extended the provisions of PCA and gave it the required edge to tackle bribery/corruption involving commercial entities/private companies. According to Section 9 of the amended Act, a commercial organization can be held liable âif any person associated with such commercial organization gives or promises to give any undue advantage to a public servantâ with an intent to obtain or retain business or any advantage for that commercial organization. This provision covers all types of entities (including domestic companies, foreign companies, and partnerships) doing business in India. Thus, while the PCA, 1988 applied to public sector employees, the Act has been amended to encompass situations where private organizations and individuals can also be held accountable for indulging in corrupt practices. Further, the CBI investigates cases of corruption in compliance with the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988, under the supervision of the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). This can include cases of bribery, extortion, and other forms of corruption. The CBI has a special division called the Anti-Corruption Branch (ACB).
